findings.text: assertOpts compares pointer addresses instead of dereferenced values: reflect.New(vt) creates new allocations at lines 140-141, so expectedValues[i].Interface() and actualValues[i].Interface() are different pointer addresses even when the functional options write identical values, causing all pointer-typed option comparisons to falsely fail.

Error formatting at line 150 uses expectedNames[i] for both expectedFmt and actualFmt, so when actualOpt differs the error message shows the expected function name for both sides, hiding which actual function was received.

assertOpts calls expectedOpts.Len() and actualOpts.Len() at lines 106 and 110 without verifying Kind() is Slice/Array first; if FunctionalOptions receives a non-slice value or assertOpts is called with non-slice actual, Len() panics.

Line 139 calls ot.In(i).Elem() assuming all functional option parameters are pointer types; if an option takes a non-pointer type (e.g., func(Config) instead of func(*Config)), Elem() panics on the non-pointer Kind.

0.reason: This finding describes the same root cause as the reference bug: reflect.New creates distinct pointer allocations for expected and actual options, so pointer-typed option values compare unequal even when functionally identical.

1.reason: The error formatting at line 150 indeed uses expectedNames[i] for both expectedFmt and actualFmt, so the actual function name is never shown in the failure message.

2.reason: assertOpts is only called from Diff with expected being a FunctionalOptionsArgument whose value is a slice (from variadic call), and actual is expected to be a slice of options; no non-slice input is plausible in the code path.

3.reason: Line 139 calls ot.In(i).Elem() without checking that the option parameter is a pointer type, so a non-pointer option parameter would cause a panic.
